'''John Albert Bindernagel''' (December 22, 1941 – January 17, 2018) was a wildlife [[biologist]] who sought evidence for [[Sasquatch]] since 1963.<ref>{{cite book
  | last = Bell
  | first = Brian
  | title = Insight Guide Pacific Northwest
  | publisher = Insight Guides
  | page = 157
  | isbn = 1-58573-150-1
| url =
 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book
  | last = Meldrum
  | first = Jeff
  | title = Sasquatch: Legend Meets Science
  | date = 4 September 2007
 | publisher =  Forge Books 
| url  =
  | page = 116
  | isbn = 978-0-7653-1217-4 }}</ref>

==Biography==
Bindernagel was born in [[Kitchener, Ontario]], attended the [[University of Guelph]] with a BSc in Biology,<ref name=Bram/> and received a PhD in Wildlife Biology from the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]], he worked as biologist of FAO, for the water, land, plants and fauna departments in several continents like Africa, Asia, Oceania, since 1995 to 2013.<ref>Mary Van de Kamp Nohl. "[https://www.milwaukeemagazine.com/pressroom/default.asp?NewMessageID=18571 Pine Lake's Bigfoot] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101229124952/http://www.milwaukeemagazine.com/pressroom/default.asp?NewMessageID=18571 |date=2010-12-29 }}". ''Milwaukee Magazine''. May 1, 2003. Retrieved on February 20, 2009.</ref> He moved to [[British Columbia]] in 1975<ref>"[https://www.milehigh.ca/archives/5.pdf Do Sasquatch really exist? On Vancouver island?]" ''The Mount Washington Marmot''. Summer 2002. p. 4. Retrieved on February 20, 2009.</ref> largely because the region was a hot spot for Bigfoot sightings.<ref name=Bram>Bram Eisenthal. "[https://www.theglobeandmail.com/servlet/story/LAC.20060401.BIGFOOT01/TPStory/National Tracking a tall tale]". ''The Globe and Mail''. April 1, 2006. Retrieved on February 20, 2009.</ref> Over the years, he collected casts of tracks that he believed belonged to Bigfoot. He also claimed to have heard the creature near [[Comox Lake]] in 1992, comparing its whooping sound to that of a [[Common chimpanzee|chimpanzee]].<ref>"Biologist believes he has found sasquatch lurking in Canada". ''Houston Chronicle''. January 23, 1994. Retrieved from ProQuest on February 20, 2009.</ref> Bindernagel believed that the Bigfoot phenomena should receive more attention from serious scientists, but remarked, "The evidence doesn't get scrutinized objectively. We can't bring the evidence to our colleagues because it's perceived as taboo."<ref>"[http://www2.canada.com/montrealgazette/news/story.html?id=21ed3436-2432-4a86-9ffe-4ea5474c8605 Fuzzy films on web hurt our cause] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111006095922/http://www2.canada.com/montrealgazette/news/story.html?id=21ed3436-2432-4a86-9ffe-4ea5474c8605 |date=2011-10-06 }}". CanWest News Service. ''Montreal Gazette''. March 24, 2007. Retrieved on February 20, 2009.</ref>

He published a book in 1998 entitled ''North America's Great Ape: The Sasquatch''.<ref>Michael Taylor. "[https://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Screams-in-the-Night-The-search-for-Bigfoot-is-2950787.php Screams in the night]". ''San Francisco Chronicle''. January 24, 1999. Retrieved on February 20, 1999.</ref> His second book, ''The Discovery of the Sasquatch: Reconciling Culture, History and Science in the Discovery Process'', was published in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://bigfootbiologist.org/page2.html|title=North America's Great Ape: the Sasquatch|last=Bindernagel|first=John|date=2016|website=Dr. John Bindernagel Homepage|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304172235/http://bigfootbiologist.org/page2.html|archive-date=March 4, 2016|url-status=}}</ref>

Bindernagel was a curator with the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization (BFRO) until his death.<ref>[https://www.bfro.net/bindernagel.asp "North America's Great Ape: the Sasquatch"]. Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization.</ref> Bindernagel died on January 17, 2018, at the age of 76. His cause of death was determined as [[cancer]].<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20180120040528/https://vancouverisland.ctvnews.ca/renowned-b-c-based-sasquatch-researcher-dies-from-cancer-1.3767992 "Renowned B.C.-based Sasquatch researcher dies from cancer"]. CTV News.</ref>

==Reception==

Bindernagel's claim that the sasquatch is a real wildlife species was not accepted by the scientific community. His book, ''North America's Great Ape: The Sasquatch'' was reviewed by James Lazell and Jeannine Caldbeck in the ''Northwestern Naturalist'' journal.<ref name="Lazell">{{cite journal|author=Lazell, James|author2=Caldbeck, Jeannine|year=2001|title=Reviewed Work: North America's Great Ape: The Sasquatch. A Wildlife Biologist Looks at the Continent's Most Misunderstood Large Mammal by J. A. Bindernagel|journal=Northwestern Naturalist|volume=82|issue=1|pages=36|doi=10.2307/3536647|jstor=3536647}}</ref> They took issue with Bindernagel's claim that many of the witness reports of the sasquatch cannot be hoaxes because this would be expensive and require a great amount of effort and time.<ref name="Lazell"/> Lazell and Caldbeck concluded:

{{blockquote|We make the point that hoaxing is vastly less expensive in energy, time and effort than actually being a real sasquatch. Any viable population of a huge ape extending, as Bindernagel claims, from the Pacific Northwest to Florida and New England, would necessarily consume such enormous resources as to be a real nuisance, make a major and unmistakable ecological impact, and be a frequent provider of road and hunter kills. Hoaxing cannot be dismissed.<ref name="Lazell"/>}}

[[Joshua Blu Buhs]] criticized Bindernagel's ''The Discovery of the Sasquatch'' for failing to prove its thesis that bigfoot exists. He wrote that Bindernagel cherry-picked his data and ignored a whole body of evidence that contradicts the idea that bigfoot is an ape-like creature.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Buhs, Joshua Blu|year=2012|title=Reviewed Work: The Discovery of the Sasquatch: Reconciling Culture, History, and Science in the Discovery Process by John A. Bindernagel, Leila Hadj‐Chikh|journal=[[Isis (journal)|Isis]]|volume=103|issue=1|pages=208–209|doi=10.1086/666446}}</ref>
